title_en: Shijia Co., Ltd. v. China Dadi Property Insurance Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over marine insurance contract
ruling_gist_en: The International Safety Management (ISM) Code is a mandatory international standard applicable to ships engaged in international voyages. If the insured vessel violates the ISM Code in the implementation of its safety management system, seriously affecting the navigation safety of the vessel, it may constitute unseaworthiness of the vessel. If such unseaworthiness has a direct causal relationship with the stranding and total loss of the vessel, the insurer shall not be liable for compensation according to law.
keywords_en: Civil; Maritime insurance contract dispute; First instance; Shanghai Maritime Court; Shanghai; Legal person; Maritime Law; Insurance Law; Determination of unseaworthiness of vessel; Violation of ISM Code and insurance liability; Whether stranding constitutes a maritime peril; Dismissal of claims; Vessel stranding; Main engine failure; Violation of the ISM Code; Total loss of vessel; Contract dispute; Insurance contract; Limited company, etc. maritime insurance contract dispute
full_text_en:
GLOBAL EMINENCE LIMITED v. China Dadi Property Insurance Co., Ltd. et al. — dispute over marine insurance contract

Ruling Summary

The International Safety Management (ISM) Code is a mandatory international standard applicable to ships engaged in international voyages. Where an insured vessel's implementation of its safety management system violates the ISM Code, thereby materially impairing the ship's navigation safety, this may constitute unseaworthiness of the vessel. If such unseaworthiness has a direct causal relationship with the stranding and total loss of the vessel, the insurer shall not be liable for compensation in accordance with the law.

Plaintiff: GLOBAL EMINENCE LIMITED. Domicile: Tortola, VG1110, British Virgin Islands.

Representative: Lin Yue'an (LAM Yuet On), Director of the Company.

Defendant: China Dadi Property Insurance Co., Ltd. Domicile: No. 1199 Minsheng Road, Pudong New Area, Shanghai, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Chen Yong, President of the Company.

Defendant: China Dadi Property Insurance Co., Ltd., Shipping Insurance Operation Center. Domicile: No. 1199 Minsheng Road, Pudong New Area, Shanghai, People's Republic of China.

Representative: Wu Yan, Deputy General Manager of the Center.

The Plaintiff, GLOBAL EMINENCE LIMITED (hereinafter "Global Eminence"), filed an action with the Shanghai Maritime Court against the Defendants, China Dadi Property Insurance Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Dadi Insurance") and China Dadi Property Insurance Co., Ltd., Shipping Insurance Operation Center (hereinafter "Dadi Insurance Shipping Center"), concerning a dispute over a marine insurance contract.

Plaintiff's Allegations:

The Plaintiff was the owner of the vessel "SAGAN" and insured it with the Defendant Dadi Insurance for a one-year ocean-going hull insurance policy in July 2016. The Defendant Dadi Insurance Shipping Center affixed the seal on the insurance policy pursuant to the authorization of Dadi Insurance and is a co-insurer. The "SAGAN" encountered sudden engine damage and severe weather in early February 2017 while en route from Kaohsiung Port, Taiwan Region, to Onsan Port, South Korea. It ran aground near Kagoshima, Japan, on February 11, 2017, and became a total loss. The Plaintiff engaged THE NIPPON SALVAGE CO., LTD. (hereinafter "Nippon Salvage") for salvage operations, incurring substantial salvage costs. The Plaintiff promptly reported the vessel's distress and salvage situation to both Defendants, but the Defendants avoided involvement in the salvage operations and refused to bear the salvage costs or compensate for the vessel's loss. Therefore, the Plaintiff requested the Court to order both Defendants: (1) to jointly and severally pay the Plaintiff the total loss compensation for the vessel in the amount of RMB 30,648,960 plus interest; (2) to jointly and severally compensate the Plaintiff for the vessel's salvage costs of USD 3,559,866.49 plus interest; and (3) to pay the case acceptance fee of RMB 166,395 and the judicial appraisal fee of RMB 75,000 in Case No. (2018) Hu 72 Min Chu 3821 (hereinafter "Case No. 3821"), and to bear the case acceptance fee in this action.

Defendant's Defense:

The grounding and loss of the vessel were not caused by the perils insured against as specified in the insurance clauses. There was no unforeseeable or unavoidable severe weather during the insured voyage. The grounding and total loss of the vessel did not constitute a loss caused by engine damage. The Plaintiff itself managed the vessel but lacked the qualifications to do so. The vessel lacked the necessary safety management system documents. The Plaintiff knew that the vessel was unseaworthy prior to departure and, after the vessel lost power, failed to take timely and effective measures to prevent or mitigate the loss. Therefore, the grounding damage was not an accident but an inevitable result, or an increased loss, and the insurer is not liable for compensation.

Facts Found by the Shanghai Maritime Court at First Instance:

The "SAGAN" was a Panama-flagged oil tanker owned by the Plaintiff, Global Eminence, and managed by Ming Jin Shipmanagement Consultant Limited (hereinafter "Mingjin Company"). Mingjin Company held a Document of Compliance (DOC), and the "SAGAN" held a Safety Management Certificate (SMC).

The ocean-going hull insurance policy was issued on July 17, 2016, with the Defendant Dadi Insurance's name on the header, affixed with the underwriting seal of the Defendant Dadi Insurance Shipping Center. The insured parties were Mingjin Company and the Plaintiff Global Eminence. The sum insured was USD 4,800,000. The insurance conditions were "Institute Time Clauses Hulls Total Loss (1/10/83), with additional cover for general average, salvage, sue and labor, and collision and contact liability." The policy period was from 00:00 on July 18, 2016, to 24:00 on July 17, 2017. Below the title of the English version of the insurance clauses, it was stated: "THIS INSURANCE IS SUBJECT TO ENGLISH LAW AND PRACTICE."

Around 1000 hours on February 1, 2017 (local time), the "SAGAN" departed from Kaohsiung Port, Taiwan Region, in ballast, bound for Onsan Port, South Korea, carrying a set of four spare piston rings. Approximately 31 hours after departure, from around 1700 hours on February 2 until 0850 hours on February 6, the main engine's scavenge air box caught fire at least seven times. Thereafter, the main engine became completely inoperable, and the vessel lost power and began drifting. On February 5, the Master inquired about instructions from the Plaintiff Global Eminence, which ordered the continuation of the voyage. At 0831 hours on February 6, the "SAGAN" reported to the Plaintiff that "the main engine cannot be started." At 1146 hours the same day, it reported that among the 24 piston rings in 6 cylinder units, only the piston rings in one cylinder unit were in good condition. On the afternoon of February 8, the Plaintiff contacted a South Korean tugboat. At 2151 hours that day, it was informed that a 5,000-horsepower tugboat was forced to return to port due to swells of 4 meters, and it was expected to depart only when the weather improved on the morning of February 11. At 2342 hours on February 9, the "SAGAN" reported to the Plaintiff that it was drifting toward Japanese islands and requested an urgent tugboat dispatch, warning that if the tugboat was delayed, the vessel might run aground. On February 10, the Plaintiff contacted a 5,000-horsepower tugboat in Japan. At 1802 hours that day, it was informed that this tugboat was expected to depart for towing the "SAGAN" only on February 13. Ultimately, after drifting for about five days, the "SAGAN" ran aground around 0600 hours local time (0500 hours Beijing time) on February 11, 2017, off the southwest coast of Suwanose Island, Japan. At 0635 hours, the Japan Coast Guard received a distress signal from the "SAGAN." At 1754 hours, the Plaintiff reported the casualty to the Defendant Dadi Insurance Shipping Center.

Nippon Salvage provided refloating services, but salvage efforts were unsuccessful. An effective judgment in Case No. 3821 ordered the Plaintiff Global Eminence to pay Nippon Salvage salvage remuneration of USD 3,559,866.49 plus interest. It was later confirmed that the "SAGAN" could be considered a constructive total loss at the time of stranding. On January 5, 2018, the registration of the "SAGAN" was cancelled. On August 4, 2018, Shin Shoji Co., Ltd. took delivery of the wreck of the "SAGAN" (including residual oil).

Opinion of the Shanghai Maritime Court at First Instance:

I. Governing Law

Below the title of the relevant Institute Time Clauses Hulls, it states: "THIS INSURANCE IS SUBJECT TO ENGLISH LAW AND PRACTICE," indicating that the interpretation of the insurance clauses should follow English law and practice. In this case, there is no other evidence proving that the parties reached an agreement on the applicable law for disputes under the insurance contract. Therefore, the law of the country with the closest connection to the contract should apply. Given that the insurer in this case is a Chinese company and the insurance contract was concluded in China, Chinese law is the law of the country with the closest connection to the insurance contract. Thus, the governing law for this case shall be the law of the People's Republic of China.

II. Cause of the Casualty

The direct cause of the total loss of the "SAGAN" was stranding. The term "stranding" is not listed as an insured peril in the relevant insurance clauses. Therefore, it is necessary to analyze specifically whether the stranding can constitute a "peril of the seas" under clause 6.1 of the insurance clauses. According to the definition of "peril of the seas" in Rule 7 of the Rules for Construction of the Policy in Schedule 1 of the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906, this term refers only to fortuitous accidents or casualties of the seas and does not include the ordinary action of the winds and waves. Consequently, not all stranding accidents automatically fall within "peril of the seas"; it is necessary to examine whether the specific stranding accident was of such a fortuitous and catastrophic nature as an "accident or casualty."

Based on the facts found, excessive wear of the main engine piston rings caused a lack of tightness between the pistons and cylinder liners, leading to main engine fires and eventual inability to start. There could be multiple possible causes for the excessive wear of the piston rings and scavenge air box fires, such as issues with the piston crowns, cylinder liners, etc. The use of low-quality fuel oil and problems with the piston rings themselves cannot be excluded. However, none of these causes constitute a "latent defect" that could not be discovered with due diligence, and there is no evidence that the casualty was caused by "any latent defect in the machinery or hull" under clause 6.2.2 of the insurance clauses. The "SAGAN" had just undergone main engine repairs and sea trials before the insured voyage. It can be reasonably presumed that the repairers and crew were negligent, failing to discover and correct the main engine problems with due diligence or failing to properly maintain the main engine. This may involve the perils of "negligence of the Master, Officers, Crew" under clause 6.2.3 and "negligence of repairers, other than the Assured" under clause 6.2.4. These are the second class of risks insured by the insurer under clause 6.2 of the insurance clauses. However, the insurer's coverage for such risks is subject to an exception proviso, namely, that the total loss of the insured subject matter is not caused by want of due diligence on the part of the Assured, Owners, or Managers.

Evidence on record shows that communication between the "SAGAN" and the Plaintiff Global Eminence was real-time and unimpeded. On February 4, the "SAGAN" reported a severe shortage of spare piston rings, urgently needing 24 piston rings. On February 5, it reported that piston rings in three out of six cylinder units were damaged. This indicates a serious shortage of spare parts onboard. If problems continued with piston rings in other cylinders, the main engine could become inoperable at any time. The Plaintiff, having the ability to rectify the vessel's unseaworthy condition, failed to take reasonable measures. It did not arrange for the urgently needed spare parts, nor did it, given the vessel's position at the time, take advantage of the main engine still being operable to divert to a nearby port for repairs. It also failed to provide adequate shore-based support to the vessel. When the Master twice inquired whether to continue the voyage, the Plaintiff instructed the "SAGAN" to proceed on the risky voyage, lacking reasonable and necessary due diligence. At 0831 hours on February 6, the Master had already reported to the Plaintiff that the main engine could not be started. The Plaintiff also learned that day that among the "SAGAN"'s six cylinder units, only the piston rings in one cylinder unit were in good condition and there were no sufficient replacement parts. It was therefore fully aware that it was impossible to restore the main engine to normal operation through crew repairs. The vessel was drifting completely without power, facing a real danger of collision and stranding. Evidence indicates that the "SAGAN" had already collided with a fishing boat on the evening of February 6. At this point, the Plaintiff should also have noted the weather forecast that sea conditions would worsen over the coming days and should have arranged for a tugboat to salvage the vessel as early as possible. However, the Plaintiff did not begin contacting a South Korean tugboat until the afternoon of February 8. Furthermore, that same day, after being informed that the tugboat had been forced to return due to high swells and was expected to depart for towing only on the morning of February 11, the Plaintiff did not immediately seek a more powerful tugboat for salvage. At midnight on February 9, the Master explicitly warned that if the tugboat was delayed, the "SAGAN" was in danger of grounding. At 0759 hours on February 10, the Plaintiff received a report that the vessel was only 60 to 70 nautical miles away from the nearest island. That day, after being informed that an alternative Japanese tugboat of the same horsepower was expected to depart only on February 13, the Plaintiff took no further emergency measures and did not instruct the vessel to send a distress signal, leaving the "SAGAN" in danger. In summary, during the process where the main engine failure of the "SAGAN" evolved into a grounding total loss, the Plaintiff lacked due diligence. Even if the main engine failure could have been caused by the second class of risks, the total loss resulted from the Plaintiff's want of due diligence. This falls within the exception where the insurer is not liable for compensation under these listed perils.

The sea conditions encountered by the "SAGAN" starting from February 9 were force 6 winds and waves of 5-6, which were better than the sea conditions on the day after departure and did not constitute disastrous abnormal sea conditions. Their effect on the "SAGAN" was "the ordinary action of the winds and waves," which would be unlikely to pose a threat to the "SAGAN" if it had normal power. Therefore, it does not constitute a "peril of the seas" under the first class of risks listed in clause 6.1 of the Institute Time Clauses Hulls.

In conclusion, the grounding total loss of the "SAGAN" was caused by the combined action of multiple causes. However, these multiple causes either did not fall within the listed perils insured by the insurer or fell within circumstances expressly excluded from coverage. Accordingly, the insurer is not liable for compensation.

III. Unseaworthiness of the Vessel

The "SAGAN" was detained during a Port State Control (PSC) inspection in July 2016, with findings of aging equipment and a recommendation for a comprehensive inspection of the vessel's condition. Prior to departure, it entered the shipyard for repairs due to main engine ignition failure. After completion of the yard repairs, it did not undergo survey and certification by the classification society. Therefore, although the "SAGAN" held a full set of valid ship certificates at the time of the incident, this is not sufficient to prove that its hull, machinery, and equipment were seaworthy. The fact that the "SAGAN"'s main engine suffered multiple scavenge air box fires starting the day after departure and ultimately lost power, rendering it unable to complete the intended voyage, is itself sufficient proof that the main engine was not in a seaworthy condition at the time of departure. On February 4, the "SAGAN" reported needing 24 spare piston rings, indicating that carrying four spare piston rings at departure may have met minimum requirements but was far from sufficient for the aging "SAGAN," which had a history of main engine failure. Therefore, the "SAGAN" was in poor condition and short of spare parts at departure, rendering it technically unseaworthy.

The "SAGAN" was detained twice consecutively during PSC inspections in April and July 2016 and was classified first as a standard risk vessel and then as a high-risk vessel. After the main engine failure, there were no effective emergency measures. The underlying reason was that the vessel had not effectively established or implemented a safety management system, making it unseaworthy in terms of safety management. The International Safety Management (ISM) Code, established by the International Maritime Organization, is an integral part of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS), 1974, and is a mandatory international standard for ships engaged on international voyages. Although the "SAGAN" held a Safety Management Certificate (SMC) and its manager, Mingjin Company, held a Document of Compliance (DOC), these are only prima facie evidence that the "SAGAN"'s safety management system complied with the ISM Code. Based on the communication between the vessel and the shore in this case, the "SAGAN" was directly operated and managed by the Plaintiff Global Eminence, which lacked ship management qualifications. Matters such as spare parts, ship repairs, and cargo safety were all under the Plaintiff's control. Mingjin Company, as the management company, never appeared. The vessel's safety management system was disconnected from actual management practices. As a result, when the main engine failed, the Plaintiff was unable to provide sufficient resources and shore-based support to the vessel as required by the ISM Code, and could not respond correctly at any time to dangers, accidents, and emergencies faced by the vessel. This caused the engine damage to gradually evolve into a grounding total loss.

In summary, the "SAGAN" was unseaworthy at the commencement of the insured voyage, both technically and in terms of its safety management system. The unseaworthiness was the cause of its grounding. The Plaintiff, as the shipowner, directly operated and managed the "SAGAN" and clearly knew of the above-mentioned problems concerning seaworthiness. Therefore, pursuant to Article 244 of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, the insurer is not liable for compensation.

Accordingly, pursuant to Articles 216, 240(1), 244(1)(1), and 268(1) of the Maritime Code of the People's Republic of China, and Article 64(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Shanghai Maritime Court rendered the following judgment on March 9, 2021:

Judgment:

The claims of the Plaintiff, GLOBAL EMINENCE LIMITED, are dismissed.

Global Eminence, dissatisfied with the first instance judgment, appealed to the Shanghai High People's Court. The grounds of appeal were: (1) The stranding accident of the vessel involved multiple fortuitous factors, including whether the vessel encountered strong winds and waves after losing power and how the Master assessed the timing and severity of the strong winds and waves were the two most significant uncertain factors, constituting accidental events. (2) The insurance clauses state "THIS INSURANCE IS SUBJECT TO ENGLISH LAW AND PRACTICE," therefore this case should be governed by English law. (3) Stranding was the proximate cause of the vessel's loss and falls within the scope of insurance coverage. (4) The first instance judgment's findings that the vessel was unseaworthy and that Global Eminence knew of the unseaworthiness distorted the facts of the case and violated evidentiary rules. The view that the vessel was unseaworthy in terms of its management status had no legal basis. In summary, Global Eminence requested the court to set aside the original judgment and render a new judgment supporting all its claims at first instance, or to remand the case for retrial.

The Respondent Dadi Insurance Shipping Center argued in defense: (1) The parties to the insurance contract did not reach an agreement to apply English law. According to the principle of closest connection, Chinese law should apply to this case. (2) The proximate cause is not the last cause in time but the decisive, effective cause. The vessel grounded under the ordinary action of wind and waves due to the fault and permissive conduct of the Appellant Global Eminence, which does not constitute an insured peril. (3) The vessel was unseaworthy before departure as it lacked a safety management system and did not carry sufficient spare parts to complete a safe voyage. (4) Global Eminence violated the ISM Code, forged key evidence such as the engine room logbook, and the actual value of the vessel was far lower than the insured value recorded in the policy, raising suspicions of insurance fraud. (5) Global Eminence failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or mitigate the loss, breaching its duty to minimize loss. The Respondent requested the Court of Second Instance to uphold the original judgment.

The Shanghai High People's Court, upon second instance trial, confirmed the facts found at first instance.

Opinion of the Shanghai High People's Court at Second Instance:

This case is a dispute over a marine insurance contract. The main issues of contention at second instance are: (1) The governing law of this case; (2) Determination of insurance liability; (3) Whether the vessel was seaworthy.

1. Applicable law of this case. The court of first instance determined that the law of the People's Republic of China is the law of the country most closely connected to the insurance contract involved in the case, and designated the law of the People's Republic of China as the applicable law of this case. This determination has a legal basis.

2. Determination of insurance liability. First, the grounding itself is not an insured risk under the insurance contract involved in the case; it is necessary to determine whether the grounding accident involved falls within the definition of the insured risk "perils of the sea." From February 9 to the occurrence of the grounding on the 11th, the wind force was Force 6, with waves of Force 5 to 6, which are normal wind and waves at sea. The main engine failure of the vessel caused the "SAGAN" to lose its ability to withstand normal wind and waves at sea. The main engine failure involved clearly does not constitute a "peril of the sea," nor does it constitute a latent defect of the vessel. Moreover, after the main engine failure occurred, if the vessel had been equipped with sufficient piston rings for replacement or had proceeded to a nearby port for repairs after the failure, the drifting situation resulting from the eventual inability to start the main engine could have been avoided. The Appellant, Shijia Company, failed to take effective measures when the main engine malfunctioned but could still be started; this is one of the causes of the grounding accident involved. Second, the master's judgment regarding the impact of wind and waves and the possibility of grounding was accurate. There was a total of five days from the vessel's drifting due to main engine failure on February 6 to the final grounding on February 11. Shijia Company, hoping to repair the main engine and continue the voyage, was imprudent and untimely in contacting tugboats and instructing the master to send distress signals, which was also one of the causes of the grounding accident involved. In summary, the Shanghai High People's Court held that, based on the evidence in the case, the grounding and total loss of the "SAGAN" resulted from a combination of multiple causes, including the main engine failure of the vessel, the shipowner's salvage measures, and the impact of wind and waves. However, none of the above causes fall within the "perils of the sea" insured under the insurance contract involved, and the insurer is not liable for compensation.

3. Whether the vessel involved was seaworthy. The ISM Code is an important component of the SOLAS Convention and applies to vessels engaged in international voyages. According to the provisions of the ISM Code, a vessel shall be operated by a company holding a Document of Compliance (DOC certificate) relevant to that vessel. The "SAGAN" was managed by the ship manager Mingjin Company, which held the DOC certificate. The vessel should have been operated by Mingjin Company. However, the evidence in the case shows that from the repair of the main engine failure to the rescue process after the vessel began drifting, Mingjin Company never appeared. Instead, the Appellant, Shijia Company, and the charterer communicated with the master. The fact that the above ship manager did not actually participate in the management of the vessel posed a serious threat to the safe navigation of the vessel, and the vessel was unseaworthy in terms of its ship safety management system. Pursuant to Article 244 of the Maritime Code, if the loss of the insured vessel is caused by its unseaworthiness at the commencement of the voyage, the insurer shall not be liable for compensation. In this case, the actual management of the vessel did not comply with the ISM Code. The unseaworthiness in the vessel's safety management system, to a certain extent, led to the failure to take effective measures after the main engine failure occurred and the untimely rescue during the subsequent drifting, ultimately causing the loss of the vessel due to grounding. The insurer is not liable for compensation for the total loss of the vessel involved.

In conclusion, the Shanghai High People's Court, pursuant to Article 177, paragraph 1, item 1, and Article 182 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on June 10, 2022, rendered the following judgment:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

This judgment is final.
